name: Yiwom

new_statements.quote: Ywom Project (2011) claims that Ywom has three level tones, but does not present an example of three-way contrast. Although many other languages in Chadic A3 do appear to have three tones, such as Mwaghavul, Ywom almost certainly has two tones and occasional mid-tones are almost certainly phonetic. Minimal pairs are as follows; wóŋ song / wòŋ to wash; mí one / mì relation; túŋ sit down / tùŋ ant-hill; túk soup / tùk to kill. There are surface glide tones, rising and falling, but there are almost certainly the output from sequences of level tones. The most striking feature of Ywom is the presence of tones on deleted vowels.
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger. 2013. Ywom wordlist. Draft circulated for comment, printout 10 September 2013. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. Section 3.3 'Tones'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ywom is described as a two-tone (H/L) language; surface mid tones are treated as phonetic and rising/falling glides as sequences of level tones; tones are retained on deleted vowels (e.g. 'two' fˊlù, 'ten' tˋrá). The source says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be extracted; only the tonal characterisation is on record.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; the tonal analysis is explicitly provisional ('almost certainly'), based on one recording (Ruth Pam, Jos, April 2012), and disputes the three-level-tone claim of Ywom Project (2011).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms from a wordlist elicitation; no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench's 'Ywom' = Yiwom yiwo1237 (also Gerka, Gerkawa, Gerkanci, Yioum); data from a single speaker (Ruth Pam) recorded in Jos, April 2012, representing the Hɨl Ywom community in Mikang LGA; no dialect division is described.

sources.note: Section 3 'Ywom phonology' (3.1 consonants, 3.2 vowels, 3.3 tones, pp. 1-5) never mentions stress or accent; 3.3 (p. 5) states Ywom 'almost certainly has two tones', mid tones phonetic, glide tones from level-tone sequences, tones survive on deleted vowels; minimal pairs given. Recovered via Wayback Machine (rogerblench.info is now a squatted domain).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2013. However did Ywom become so strange? Slides presented at BICCL 7, Hamburg, 12-14 September 2013, Asien-Afrika-Institut, Hamburg University. 34 slides.
sources.note: Slides 'Ywom Phonology I-XV' cover consonants, labial-velars, vowels, length, vowel deletion and tone; slide 21 ('Ywom Phonology XIV') repeats the two-tone statement verbatim. No mention of stress, accent or prominence. Recovered via Wayback Machine.
